title: London commuters braced for disruption as tube strike begins
summary:
Industrial action by RMT drivers expected to cause severe disruption on Thursday and Friday

Severe disruption is expected across the London Underground on Thursday and Friday, when many tube…

blocks.text: Severe disruption is expected across the London Underground on Thursday and Friday, when many tube drivers will go on strike.

Drivers who are part of the national union of rail, maritime and transport workers (RMT) will strike for 24 hours from noon on Thursday, in the first of a fresh wave of strikes in the long-running dispute over the planned introduction of a four-day working week.
Talks to avert the strike ended at the Acas conciliation service on Tuesday without resolution.
The RMT has planned seven more strike dates, including two 24-hour stoppages in the week before Christmas, which will affect transport during four of the busiest shopping days in the capital.
The union, which represents just under half of tube drivers, claimed that the changes to working patterns were being imposed and could lead to increased fatigue and affect safety.

London Underground said the changes were voluntary, and the strike has been described as “strange” by the rival drivers’ union. Aslef, a union representing a slight majority of Tube drivers, warmly welcomed the proposal for a shorter working week.

Transport for London (TfL) warned passengers to plan ahead and expect disruption on all lines. Most tube lines will continue to operate on Thursday, aside from the Piccadilly and Circle lines. The Waterloo & City line will be closed from midday.
Reduced services are expected across the rest of the tube network from late morning on Thursday and will finish earlier in the evening. No service is expected after 9pm.
On Friday, trains will start running later than usual, from about 7am, and remain disrupted through the afternoon, with normal services only expected to resume by early evening.

The Elizabeth line, London Overground and national rail services will run as usual, but are expected to be crowded. Buses are not directly affected, but are likely to be busier than usual and slowed by increased congestion on the roads.

blocks.caption: Normal service is expected to resume by early evening on Friday. Photograph: James Manning/PA

blocks.text: Nick Dent, director of customer operations for London Underground, said the strike was disappointing, after months of discussions about the voluntary proposals. He said London Underground had provided the option to address the RMT concerns to “give our colleagues a real, meaningful choice on their working pattern without having to change where they work.

“Drivers who choose a four-day week, and those who choose to work a five-day pattern with the same terms and conditions as the four-day pattern, will spend less time at work per year, while delivering a more efficient, reliable Tube service for our customers,” he said. “We continue to believe that the majority of the concerns from the RMT have now been resolved and we urge the RMT to put this proposal to their members.”

The RMT said it had not been given the assurances it was seeking. The general secretary, Eddie Dempsey, said: “There is nothing voluntary about a scheme that forces drivers to give up existing protections whether they work four days or five and threatens those who refuse with displacement from their depots.
“Our members are being asked to spend more time driving trains, accept longer and more unpredictable shifts and surrender agreements that have been negotiated and defended over many years.
“This is not about improving work-life balance. It is about squeezing more work out of fewer drivers while giving management greater flexibility at the expense of our members.”

No further talks are expected before the strike. RMT’s next strikes are planned for Thursday 17 and Saturday 19 December, which businesses have said could significantly impact four days over the busiest shopping and entertainment weekend before Christmas.
Further strikes are planned immediately on the wider return to work in the New Year, on Monday 4 January and Wednesday 6 January 2027, with three more strikes scheduled in February.

Separately, some Eurostar services between London and Paris were cancelled on Wednesday because of unexpected strike action by some staff. Eurostar said the surprise industrial action, which came during annual pay talks, meant it was “experiencing cancellations and severe disruption”.
